text: Every gate you've met so far acts on exactly one qubit. CNOT is the first gate that genuinely needs two: it's where thinking of a quantum computer as two independent single-qubit circuits running side by side stops being accurate.

CNOT, controlled-NOT, acts on a control qubit and a target qubit. Ordering the two-qubit basis as ket-00, ket-01, ket-10, ket-11, with q1 as control and q2 as target: CNOT on ket-00 and ket-01 leaves them untouched, since the control is 0. CNOT on ket-10 gives ket-11, and CNOT on ket-11 gives ket-10, since the control is 1 and the target flips. Only the target's bit ever changes, and only where the control bit is 1.

Multiplying the CNOT matrix by itself gives back the identity exactly, so CNOT is its own inverse — apply it twice under the same condition and you undo the first flip. And it's not just X applied to both qubits: X on both qubits unconditionally flips ket-10 to ket-01, while CNOT turns ket-10 into ket-11 — genuinely different gates on the same input. CNOT can't be written as a product of two independent single-qubit gates at all, and that non-factorizability is exactly what makes it capable of entangling qubits.

Here's a detail worth sitting with before the next lesson: CNOT applied to any of the four basis states always outputs another single basis state, never a superposition. A basis state like ket-10 already has no uncertainty to correlate, so CNOT turning it into ket-11 is still just as separable — no entanglement yet. Entanglement only appears when CNOT acts on a superposition across the control qubit, which is exactly what Lesson 13 builds.
Next lesson generalizes CNOT into a full recipe: take any single-qubit gate and build a controlled version of it that acts on the target only when the control is 1.
